effective_layers.text: This movement originated in the Western Qin Great Revolution of 1810. People of this age viewed it as a modern economic transformation arising within agrarian eastern societies rooted in clan structures. Its method was to confiscate or redeem over-concentrated land from old owners and redistribute it among peasants, thereby freeing resources to the market. In politics, the reforms aim to grab power from old military nobles by physically reduce their wealth and means to control their 'clansmen'. As Northern Ming nobilities, with their highly militarised tradition in local ruling, are widely regarded as the source of chaos and poverty among the people of the old northern regimes. The Chinese imperial ruling bloc once suspended this transformation during its rise. But around Mu Zhongtang's 1820 southern campaign, to revive the economy, liberate production, and mobilize peasants and soldiers from the bottom, Mu and his confidants reopened the movement.

Everything should have remained so...

In 1819, after founding emperor Mu Zhongtang and his military meritorious allies completed 'the land purge' across all North China, the empire replaced the republic to public acclaim. At this moment of peril, the founding emperor decisively revived the slogan of 'land rights revolution'. Land reorganization profits and population mobility stabilized a faltering imperial economy. 牧仲棠的小妹牧沐子比兄长年轻近二十岁。生性聪明，长而端庄，胸有忠志。在牧仲棠晚年独得宠爱，不仅地位高于后宫诸女，更常常代因为襄阳旧伤而腿脚不便的皇帝劳军料民。牧仲棠甚至派遣自己的京营大将费西翼往来护送。这位长公主因此拥有了很大的威望。而在牧仲棠去世后，她挺身而出维护国政稳定，实位列于扶龙功臣之列。

然而，稳定后宫、安定军民，这样重要的角色由新君的姑姑担任，不由得让东方帝国的权臣勋旧们纷纷想起了太平公主的故事。加之汴梁城郊东苑的文官之间，难免有许多心存更共和的理想者对于这位亲民贵族抱有期待。因此，帝国枢密院的武勋故旧老臣们最终一致决定——以一种温和的方式将这位大人及其他不安定分子移出决策圈外。

于是，在一心退休的帝国元勋大将费西翼“表率”下，一干曾经的京营老臣“护送”牧沐子往东洲国“旅行居住”。从此以后再未回到牧氏华朝。

before:
Mu Muzi, younger sister of Mu Zhongtang, was nearly twenty years younger than her brother. Bright and dignified, she held steadfast loyalty. In Mu's later years she was uniquely favored: above all palace women, and often acting in his place to inspect armies and aid civilians when old Xiangyang wounds limited his mobility. Mu even assigned his capital-camp general Fei Xiyi to escort her, giving the princess great prestige. After Mu's death, she stepped forward to stabilize state affairs and stood among the foremost contributors to succession order.

Yet for the emperor's aunt to hold such authority over palace stability and military-civil peace inevitably reminded powerful old courtiers of Princess Taiping's precedent. In addition, many civil officials in the East Garden outside Bianliang - some nurturing more republican ideals - placed hopes in this populist noblewoman. Ultimately, veteran military elders of the Privy Council agreed to remove her and other unstable elements from decision-making by a 'gentle' method.

Thus, under the 'example' of retiring imperial marshal Fei Xiyi, a group of former capital-camp elders 'escorted' Mu Muzi to reside in the Eastern Continent as a long-term 'traveler.' She never returned to Mu Hua rule again.

before: Chronicles of the Northern Ming Warring States is a late-life novel by Mu Muzi, younger sister of founder Mu Zhongtang, written after the Chinese Great Revolution in the Northern Ming world. The work spans five major and ten minor volumes, 480 chapters, and nearly two million characters, with a composition period of thirty-five years. Mu Muzi departed from chaptered-serial conventions and rigid portrayals of princes and generals, drawing on the narrative strengths of classics such as Water Margin, Strange Tales, and Journey to the West to shape characters from every class and stratum of society. In a near-modern historical style, the book recounts over four centuries from the sudden death of Yongle in a 1408 hunt to the 1835 Treaty of Yangzhou and the north-south river partition. Because the work 'bears history's weight while transforming it with the spirit of fiction,' and 'tells both Chinese heroism and old-age suffering,' and is 'required reading for anyone seeking the roots of Asian modernity,' later generations ranked it among the Five Great Chinese Classics and one of the longest novels in human history.

after: The streets of [SCOPE.sState('cne_land_reform_peasants_in_city_state').GetName] are filling with newcomers from the countryside. Farming families have sold their land and come in search of wages. Employment brokers send them to factories and building sites, deducting recruitment and lodging charges from their pay.\n\nWorkers have accused the brokers of withholding contracts and enforcing old debts. Manufacturers fear that an inquiry will disrupt recruitment, while local gentry defend brokers linked to their own associations. The governor must decide whether to prosecute the organisations that bind workers to them or leave the disputes to ordinary civil proceedings. In these growing towns, the promise that peasants could leave their old estates and freely earn a living faces its first practical tests.

The senior commanders and ministers of the Senate propose a compromise and ask [ROOT.GetCountry.GetRuler.GetFullNameWithTitle] to close the campaign by decree. Under their draft, land recognised by the new deeds would remain with military households, who must promise lower rents and allow tenants to leave for work.
